name: Cannabis use disorder

icd11.label: Harmful pattern of use of cannabis

dsmPointer: See DSM-5-TR: Substance-Related and Addictive Disorders — Cannabis Use Disorder
summary: A pattern, described in ICD-11 terms, in which cannabis use slips out of the client's control and takes priority over work, study, relationships, mood and safety, sometimes with craving and an uncomfortable withdrawal (irritability, poor sleep, low appetite, restlessness) on stopping. Daily use of high-potency products has grown, and heavy use is linked to anxiety, worse mood and, in some people, psychosis. Motivational, cognitive-behavioral and incentive-based approaches help; set goals with the client, including reduction where abstinence is not their aim. Substance-use information is protected: nothing here is stored or sent, and every export carries the Part 2 notice. 42 CFR Part 2 prohibits unauthorized use or disclosure of these records. For clinician review only; this is not a diagnosis.

durationGate.note: Ask about the pattern of use over the past year, including attempts to stop. DSM-5-TR and ICD-11 both look at the pattern over months; check the timing they describe.

ruleOuts.label: Other substance use
ruleOuts.note: Ask about alcohol, nicotine and other drugs; combined use changes the plan. This app does not store or send substance-use information.

ruleOuts.label: Cannabinoid hyperemesis and other medical effects
ruleOuts.note: Repeated vomiting with heavy use, lung symptoms from smoking and heart effects need medical review.

ruleOuts.label: Anxiety, mood or psychotic disorders
ruleOuts.note: Ask whether symptoms came before heavy use or continue during sober periods.

specifiers.label: ICD-10-CM coding notes
specifiers.note: F12.1x codes a harmful (abuse) pattern and F12.2x a dependence pattern, each with remission and withdrawal codes. DSM-5-TR uses its own severity and course specifiers with these codes: See DSM-5-TR.

specifiers.label: ICD-11 coding notes
specifiers.note: 6C41.1 is a harmful pattern of use of cannabis and 6C41.2 is cannabis dependence. Check the WHO ICD-11 browser for current qualifiers.

differentials.label: Cannabis-induced anxiety or psychotic disorder
differentials.distinguishing: Symptoms arise during heavy use and ease with abstinence.

differentials.label: Generalized anxiety disorder
differentials.distinguishing: Worry came first and continues during sober periods.

differentials.label: Major depressive disorder
differentials.distinguishing: Low mood continues during sober periods.

comorbidities.label: Anxiety
comorbidities.note: Cannabis is often used to manage anxiety; withdrawal can worsen it at first.

comorbidities.label: Psychosis
comorbidities.note: Heavy, high-potency use is linked to higher risk of psychosis and relapse.

comorbidities.label: Adult ADHD
comorbidities.note: Higher rates of cannabis use; assess attention history.

interventions.name: Motivational enhancement and CBT
interventions.evidence: A Cochrane review (Gates et al., 2016) found that CBT, motivational enhancement and their combination reduced use.
interventions.note: Explore the client's goals, build coping and refusal skills.

interventions.name: Contingency management (program-based)
interventions.evidence: Gates et al. (2016) found added incentives improved outcomes in some trials.
interventions.note: Refer to programs that offer it.

interventions.name: Relapse prevention planning
interventions.evidence: Part of CBT for substance use (NICE CG51 covers psychosocial approaches for drug misuse).
interventions.note: Plan for high-risk situations and slips.

interventions.name: Sleep and withdrawal support
interventions.evidence: Poor sleep is a common reason for returning to use.
interventions.note: Plan sleep habits and coping for the first weeks.

culturalNotes: Norms about cannabis, prescription pills and other drugs vary widely, and legal status differs by state and country. Anchor the assessment in control and harm, not in legal status or amounts alone.

Stigma, fear of losing custody, housing, work or immigration status, and past experiences with police can make clients cautious. Explain confidentiality, its limits and 42 CFR Part 2 protections plainly.
Use person-first, non-judgmental language (a person who uses drugs, not an addict) and offer harm-reduction options alongside abstinence goals.
Culturally grounded and community-led programs, including Indigenous healing approaches and peer recovery services, are often more acceptable; ask what support looks like for the client.

Faith can be a strong support in recovery. Offer faith-based groups or faith-integrated approaches only when the client asks and after informed consent (see the AACC Code of Ethics for faith-based counselors).
Use a trained professional interpreter, not family members, and check that key terms translate with the meaning you intend.

redFlagRules.message: Suicide-related content is documented in this input. Substance use raises suicide risk, especially during intoxication, withdrawal or after a loss; ask directly, include substances and other means in safety planning, and follow your risk protocol.
Psychotic symptoms are documented. Substance-induced psychosis and withdrawal delirium need urgent medical and psychiatric evaluation.
